# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movies where main character lives alone in modern times

**Score:** 31
**Body:** Looking for stories(book or movie) of deeply complex older character (female preferred) that because of who they are, maybe the stigmas of society, maybe they live outside the norms...lives alone. could also be because they don't trust people because of the damage they carry, or they just choose this path. Thanks AND No Apocalypse movies, no Horror movies please.   Example : nomadland, I also really enjoyed "Dispatches from elsewhere" I want to add.. deep character and of deep strength...maybe miss understood. ya.. I know

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Leave No Trace is an excellent film though the older character is male but it also has an excellent younger female character.
2. Book not movie but highly recommend "Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of The Dead" by Olga Tokarczuk. Not horror. Very deep "old woman lives alone" vibes.
3. You might try:

Land (2021)  
Wendy and Lucy  
Trucker
  - Land was great!
4. Allison Janney did a film called Lou and I loved it because she lived alone in a forest and was curmudgeon-like...for GOOD reason. She was also badass...
5. Wild (2024)

Tracks (2013)

Contact (1997) ??
6. Perfect Days, dir. Wim Wenders. A fairly solitary character, but a lovely meditation on his solitude. Very grounded in everyday life. 
7. A Man Called Ove

Its a wonderful book and a great movie. A remake was made for American audiences called A Man Called Otto. 
8. The Collected Regrets of Clover (it's a book)
9. Call Me Chihiro (2023) absolutely stunning, amazing, I could rant about this movie. It’s about loneliness in the most intimate of ways. One of the best endings I’ve seen that don’t just turn around and say “well she’s happy now because she’s in love and doesn’t live alone anymore”. 

Also, very subjective, but if you like musicals/comedy, Bo Burnhams Inside (2021). During the pandemic he shot a documentary style one man comedy while alone in his guest house. It definitely hit a lot harder during the pandemic, and you might recognize a lot of the songs because of how popular they got, but it’s still a really good insight into loneliness and the modern world. 

## 2. Looking for a steamy, sensual movie with a story that actually hooks me (any language, any genre)

**Score:** 32
**Body:** Home alone tonight and in the mood for something bold and sexy, but I don't want a movie where the story is an afterthought. I want something that grabs me in the first 10 minutes and keeps me hooked till the end.

Any genre works: thriller, horror, drama, romance, whatever. Indian or international, both are fine. Just no softcore stuff with zero plot.

One request: please keep it to your top 1-3 picks so I'm not scrolling forever. For each one, tell me:

Sexiness/boldness: x/10

Story: x/10

One line on why it's worth watching (no spoilers!)

Thanks in advance!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Body Heat
  - This is the one.  10/10 and 10/10 on OP’s scales.  One line reason to watch?  The story is unpredictable, engaging, and full of surprises and Kathleen Turner is phenomenal in it.
2. Bound
3. Unfaithful (2002)
4. Secretary
5. I always go with "The Thomas Crown Affair" Pierce Brosnan version.

One line: Pierce Brosnan and Rene Russo are in this and their chemistry has no match.
6. The Handmaiden
7. 3 from me. I will not give away plot spoilers so 'why it's worth watching' is sparse, but including the literary works they are based on to give a clue.

**1/ Lust, Caution (2007)**

Sexiness/Boldness: 10/10

Story: 10/10

Why it's worth watching: Ang Lee’s masterful, slow-burn espionage WW2-era Chinese-set thriller. Based on an Eileen Chang short story.

**2/ Eyes Wide Shut (1999)**

Sexiness/Boldness: 9/10

Story: 9/10

Stanley Kubrick’s final film. Surreal, dreamlike nocturnal odyssey. Based on the novella 'Dream Story' by Austrian writer Arthur Schnitzler (but transposed to NYC).

**3/ The Pillow Book (1996)**

Sexiness/Boldness: 10/10

Story: 8/10

It's Peter Greenaway, of course it's sexy. Visually hypnotic art piece involving erotic calligraphy. Has a loose connection with 'The Pillow Book of Sei Shonagon'.
8. Y tu mama tambien
9. Cat People 1982

## 3. Big Budget box office flubs that are still a fun ride?

**Score:** 30
**Body:** Clicked some dumb MSN article about a big budget sci-fi/fantasy that failed with the critics/people, but according to the article 'deserved another look.' was arthur, legend of the sword. I like Guy Ritchie and Charlie, and never knew it existed. Was a ton of fun if you didn't look too deeply. amazing cast, great sets, good though kinda ridiculous action, cool CGI and magic use, and some good humor. kind of a goofy re-imagination, but that's beside the point. It's not on any of my top lists, but had a very enjoyable two hours in this other world. Any other movies like this, that maybe don't have the most airtight story, maybe seen as disappointments, but are still a treat for the senses?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I still love The Thirteenth Warrior
2. John Carter

Alita 

Speed Racer

Waterworld
3. I really liked the Sorcerers Apprentice (2010).  It barely made over its budget, and critics have rated it quite poorly.

But it was fun.  And an interesting concept that magic is just extreme science.
4. Dark City
5. "The Adventures of Baron Munchausen" (1988)
  - I get that it’s not for everyone but I think it’s a masterpiece.
6. The Island
7. John Carter might have died a horrible death at the box office, but was impressive in parts and deserved better.
8. The Spawn movie is pretty good, even though it didn't do that well when it was originally released. John Leguizamo as the Violator is actually one of the highlights of the movie on rewatches.
9. Blade Runner 2049 is the greatest example of this. My favourite movie of all time, love it so goddamn much.

## 4. What should I watch if I loved Lost in Translation (2003)

**Score:** 28
**Body:** I'm looking for films that captured the very specific feelings that Lost in Translation gave me. It's hard for me to describe it but the movie really made me feel the connections between characters, the quiet solace that they gave each other, the feeling of loneliness, being adrift in a foreign land, with great soundtrack and an almost dream like atmosphere that enhanced the story. I wanna see movies like those, sink into them and feel everything

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. In the Mood for Love
2. *Drive My Car* (2021)
3. Paterson
4. Her
5. Columbus (2017) is the closest on mood. Two lonely people in a small Indiana town, a quiet friendship, slow and dreamy with a soft ambient score.

Before Sunrise (1995) for the adrift-in-a-foreign-city part. Two strangers get off a train in Vienna and talk until morning.

The Lunchbox (2013) if you'll go a bit warmer. Two lonely people in Mumbai who only reach each other through notes in a lunch tin, with the same quiet solace.
6. Chungking Express (1994)
7. Perfect Days
8. Rental Family has a similar vibe with a Japanese backdrop to boot.
9. *In the mood for love,* instantly came to my mind. 
10. Grand Hotel 1932 

Before Sunrise

The Apartment 

Elizabethtown 

Holiday 

Remember the Night

Cleo from 5 to 7 

Groundhog Day 

Magnolia

The Virgin Suicides 

500 Days of Summer 

Past Lives 

Smiles of a Summer Night

Stranger than Fiction 

Midnight in Paris 

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind 

Licorice Pizza

Phantom Thread

## 5. Fun but scary horror movies to watch with friends

**Score:** 28
**Body:** I’m not looking for “so bad it’s good” movies or movies that are considered fun horror like spoofs, really cheesy ones, etc. But I also don’t want anything that’s too quiet, slow and serious (for example we watched lake mungo together and although it’s a great movie we didn’t enjoy watching it as a group that much).  
I want the middle ground, movies that wouldn’t be ruined by us talking over it at certain points and that have annoying dumb characters we can make fun of but that also have good jumpscares, gore, or anything that will make us tense. Alternatively, we could also be into something darker to watch more seriously without making fun of, but it would have to be something really scary and creepy with a great story and still it can’t be that much of a slow burn.

For reference, here are a few of the movies we’ve watched together that were the most fun:  
\- creep  
\- as above so below  
\- the borderlands  
\- banshee chapter  
\- gonjiam   
\- the ritual   
\- incantation   
and hell house 1 and 4, last shift and deadstream are ones I watched by myself but would fit the type of movie i’m looking for 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I mean, when it comes to gore and fun at the same time, no-one did it better than Tucker and Dale VS Evil 
  - But it’s not scary
2. Late Night With the Devil is genuinely such a fun, scary movie. Probably my favourite horror movie. Would love to rewatch with some friends if I ever make ‘em. 
3. Trick or Treat
4. Ready or not

The menu
5. My friends and I looooved The Descent when we were in high school!
6. Zombieland

Mandy

Slither
7. Cabin in the Woods

Hatchet
8. BARBARIAN 
9. the visit

## 4. Robert Zemeckis and Jennifer Lopez Clashing Over Final Cut of Netflix’s $100M-Costing ‘The Last Mrs. Parrish’

**Score:** 157
**Body:** >What the hell is going on over at Netflix? We have already seen reports of behind-the-scenes drama around Greta Gerwig, David Fincher and Ben Affleck’s latest films — now it’s Robert Zemeckis? 

>Here's a story from Page Six Hollywood involving Jennifer Lopez who is reportedly clashing with Robert Zemeckis over the cut of "The Last Mrs. Parrish," Netflix's $100M adaptation of Liv Constantine's bestselling thriller.

>According to multiple sources, the film has been testing poorly, and Lopez, who also produces, has decided to involve herself in the editing room. One source didn't hold back: "She's tried to take it over. She fancies herself a filmmaker." lol. 

>Another said everyone behind the scenes is calling it a Blake Lively situation, a reference to the "It Ends With Us" cut war that eventually spiraled into the Lively-Baldoni legal mess.

>Netflix's official statement? The film "tested well, particularly with fans of Jennifer." A joint statement from Netflix, Lopez and Zemeckis went further, calling the reporting "categorically false" and insisting Lopez and Zemeckis are working in unison.

>Zemeckis hasn't had a genuine critical or commercial win in a long time. "Welcome to Marwen," "The Witches," "Pinocchio" and "Here" all came and went, and "Here" in particular was a boxoffice bomb despite reuniting him with Tom Hanks. Netflix somehow thought it was a good idea to give Zemeckis $100M for a Jennifer Lopez-starring movie. It's now in post-production trouble.

>The cast also includes Isabel May as the con artist targeting a wealthy couple, played by Lopez and Nikolaj Coster-Waldau. Cameras started rolling in September 2025, and the film is now not expected until sometime in 2027.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. A real shame that it has come down to this for Zemeckis. 
  - Yeah, I wish he’d stopped with “Allied” in 2016. The man has made some of my favorite movies of all time (BTTF, Roger Rabbit, Forest Gump, Contact) but it’s been mostly turds for the last decade. I didn’t think “Here” was bad, just kinda gimmicky. But Marween, Witches and Pinocchio are simply bad films. Dookie. Maybe he should just produce going forward?
    - I can't believe he still gets 100mil budget films

His last great movie was Flight
    - People around these parts get really, really angry at Quentin Tarantino for deciding to do only 10 movies, but it's like... he's seen this happen a million times with directors. 

Are there people like Scorsese still doing excellent work at the end of their life? Yes. But there's plenty, \*plenty\* of directors who with hindsight should have left it on this high or that flick, but instead have a filmography where the last few entries are generic, borderline work-for-hire fluff. If you're someone who just wants to provide money for your family, there's nothing wrong with that, but if you're a guy like Tarantino who clearly cares about his legacy, that is a "bad future."

"Let's go out on top while you're still loved, and then spending your later years doing books, plays, and TV shows" has always made sense to me. I know Reddit isn't a collective, but it's just funny to me to see one person say, "This director should have gone out on this," but then see other people get so, so mad when someone preemptively makes that choice.
2. So you have the Zemeckis cut and the Lopez cut and put them both up for the audience to choose the better of the two.
3. Netflix should stop spending 1-200m on mediocre attempts to score big, and start making mid-budget, $30-40m RomComs, dramas and romances that have been sorely missing from the cinemas.

Audiences would love another When Harry Met Sally, or The Hangover, or Good Will Hunting or The Sixth Sense - the kind of films that don't get proper cinema releases anymore. And they could make 5 or six of them for the price of one Red Notice.
4. As someone who definitely HAS NOT test screened this movie, and therefore DID NOT sign an NDA barring me from sharing my thoughts on it (which I wouldn't have any, cause again, HAVEN'T SEEN IT), I feel pretty comfortable saying that I would've found it weirdly charming for how offensively bad it probably is. 

But now that I know they're trying to fix it, I sure am glad I did not get to screen the early version. That would've been too much fun.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Some quick thoughts on NAZA

**Score:** 90
**Body:** Just got out of a screening for NAZA. NAZA is a documentary about how Israel uses artificial intelligence and massive phone surveillance to conduct strikes on Hamas targets while they are at home. 

The core of the documentary is that the Hamas targets ARE AT HOME. This necessitates that there will be collateral damage, which the Israeli military/intelligence refer to as naza, or an estimate of how many civilians would be killed. I will use lowercase when referring to collateral damage, and uppercase NAZA when referring to the film. 

In NAZA, one of the codirectors, Yuval, interviews intelligence agents who conducted or contributed to these home drone strikes in some form or fashion. The interviews take place at night, on top of a roof deck of a building in Tel Aviv. Yuval is visible, but the agents have had their appearance and voices changed, and they talk from the shadows. 

The agents reveal how systematic their AI and surveillance systems are. In several instances, agents confirmed the presence of a Hamas target by listening to their cell phones and hearing something like "Daddy's home." To drive the point home, they knew that confirming the target's presence in this manner would result in wiping out young children. 

Targets are quantified by their naza. But this is not to suggest that there's any care or concern. Any target with naza under 20 was basically automatic approval, even if they were a new recruit or essentially a nobody. Some targets had naza in the hundreds! That required go ahead from higher-ups, but they were greenlit. 

One of the architects of this surveillance system admitted that it is only about 85% accurate. But he argues that it's better to outsource these decisions to an unemotional algorithm than to an enraged Israeli. 

More broadly, there's a persistent theme across the agents of "I'm just a cog" or "if I don't do it, someone else will." Others are a bit more forthright, with one agent admitting that he partook in a genocide. Yuval asks him: when did you have this revelation? The agent said he didn't really have it during his service time. While he was an agent, he was locked in, everything was about mission accomplished, and at one point, he even said it was fun. 

A very stark picture is drawn here. These intelligence agents are upper middle class. They are not outwardly sycophantic or bloodthirsty. They are smart, capable, and efficient. A few agents even admit their units did not have "Arab haters." To which Yuval notes "it's weird that the non Arab haters have killed the most Arabs" and there's no thoughtful reply given. The agents do not come across as remorseful, or wracked with guilt. They are detached, steely in many cases. 

Yuval's interviewing style is worth discussing as well. Typically, he asks a straightforward question and the agents give pretty honest-seeming answers. In particular, the answers are straightforward as well. There's no spin after the fact. Yuval has to prod them to get them to say "I'm just a cog." As in, the agents don't say "I approved drone strikes that killed thousands of civilians---BUT I'M JUST A COG." No. There's no emotional charge. Like I said above, the agents are steely. My read on this is...all of this is too fresh. These agents, even the ones who agreed to be interviewed for NAZA, may not fully grasp what they have done until some years have passed. 

Finally, what I want to discuss is the cinematic aspect of this documentary. I think the way Yuval and his codirector Rachel structured this documentary is masterful. 

Let me reset the picture. The documentary is essentially Yuval interviewing Israeli agents on a roof top in Tel Aviv. Yuval is visible, the agents in the shadows. But that's not the static shot. No. They will pan around the skyline and show you Israelis in their skyrise apartments, with their shades either opened or only partially closed. Cooking food, watching TV, stretching, petting their dogs. Just going about their lives. 

These candid shots of people would be otherwise mundane. But when they serve as the backdrop of a cloaked Israeli agent systematically mapping out, Yuval had a lot of them literally draw out what they saw on their drone programs, how they conducted strikes on apartment buildings, just WOW. 

Edit: In particular, Yuval is putting us the viewer in the shoes of the agents, who monitor everything through a drone camera. We see what they see right before they call in one of these drone strikes. 

It all builds up to the last sequence. Up until now, all we really saw were the interviews and the Tel Aviv skyline, occassionally some beach shots, mixed in with some news footage of Netanyahu. Up until the last few minutes, we do not see any Gazan devastation. And we finally cut to it at the end. A building completely decimated, dead bodies in the rubble.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I can’t recall a documentary that has left with more of a visceral, physical reaction than NAZA. I felt physically ill afterwards, my stomach was churning. When credits rolled, the theatre was silent except sniffles.

At its core, the film is about dehumanization and how war technologies enable it by removing the person. This is the outcome when war becomes gamified: targets are pre-determined by imperfect algorithms, civilian casualties are reduced to statistics, violence is abstracted through screens. This should be a chilling warning for anyone watching to be wary of the shift towards AI military warfare.

The banality of evil is in full effect - you can tell Glazer’s production influence based on the similarities to the Zone of Interest. You spend the film watching the comforts of Israeli homes, the homes that the intelligence officers returned to, not so different from the homes kilometers away that they destroyed through buttons on a screen. The true horror of war is only displayed in the last moments. The saddest part is evidenced within this very comment section - those who will discredit it without ever having seen it have the most to gain by watching it.
2. The voyeuristic shots peering into random peoples' apartments and lives really communicate the idea of an all seeing apparatus that can select a target without their knowledge and destroy it at will. Chilling. 
  - Made total sense the movie was executive produced by Jonathan Glazer (director of Zone of interest)
3. All these occupation soldiers seem to have forgotten their own history. The Nuremberg Trials established that following orders is not a valid defense against war crimes. They are all "cogs" that their superiors depend upon to carry out the massacres.

And even with all this, still Netenyahu's block got the most number of seats in the recent election. An election where the so called "opposition" has the same position on the Genocide and a 2SS as his. 

The rot you see in the film permeats every part of Israeli society. If this is what made it into the film and public conscience, imagine what does not.
4. I have family killed during the Holocaust, and had watched documentaries and read countless books about it since I was first told about it. This movie left me with the same feeling of how apathetic evil truly is
5. Good film. As someone who had to study international law as part of my LLM it shows the reality of international humanitarian law. You cant make the law too strict because otherwise no one would follow it but on the other hand keeping it as it is makes killing 20 civilians for 1 combatant justified(depending on the circumstances). 

Not defending israels behaviour btw just sad about the state of ihl. 
6. I find it very problematic that the filmmakers relied entirely on anonymous sources and made no attempt to corroborate anything. 


Because of this, I'm not even sure whether this can be classified as a documentary. In my mind, a higher standard of research is required for that designation
  - Israeli government is already trying to track those interviewed anonymously in the documentary. 

[**Netanyahu Orders Investigation and Prosecution of Israeli Soldiers in NAZA**](https://truthout.org/articles/netanyahu-orders-investigation-and-prosecution-of-israeli-soldiers-in-naza/)
  - What problems did you have with specific conclusions it drew?
  - When public reporting is based on anonymous sources, the credibility of the journalist is paramount. Unfortunately for this film, its creators don’t exactly have a great track record. They were responsible for the lie that ‘IDF figures show 83% of deaths are civilians’ when the story actually was that the combatants whose biographies the IDF were able to fully identify comprised 17% of the death toll. This does not even come close to meaning every single other death was a civilian, that is a totally absurd standard that has never been and never will be applied to any other conflict.

## 2. Digger - the film is literally performing inception on us

**Score:** 46
**Body:** You noticed that Inceptionesque "BWOOONG" sound in the middle of the movie, right? The foghorn-like noise that tells everyone we need to go deeper? Yeah, that's not a coincidence. And it's not a coincidence that the song playing at the end of the film has French lyrics like the Edith Piaf song in Inception.

Here's what's going on: two levels down, we are being presented with the idea of climate collapse through the farce that is the play called "Fossil Fools". At this point it's absurd the way nuclear holocaust is in Dr. Strangelove, and it lulls us into a false sense of security by giving audiences exactly what they expected from the trailer: a hammy satire poking fun at conservative politicians, Texas oilmen, and anti-science evangelicals.

But when the tree falls and the giant man pops up from behind the hill, the illusion is destroyed and we're transported to the next level up. During these scenes the characters struggle with a question: how should climate collapse be portrayed? Whatever is going on, it's no longer a farce; we're forced to accept the reality of climate collapse (in the film's universe) because the play is recounting "real" events.

And that's why the film ends the way it does, with "Level 4" warning the theatre-goers to don their masks before stepping out into a dystopian world. It's supposed to be a gut-punch when the doors open, because we've gone from climate collapse as farce, to climate collapse as an academic question about art, to climate collapse as the daily reality of the actors and audience. When "Level 4" again blares out in our IRL theatres, it's going up to the "top level" as it were, where we ourselves are exiting the theatre and it's no longer a dream. The film is using the layers portrayed in Inception to plant an idea - climate collapse is real - and to gradually reinforce it as we move up level by level.

But it goes deeper than that. "Inception" introduces the idea that Dom himself is deceived; that while he believes he is the one executing the heist and that Fischer is his mark, it is Dom himself who is being led out of a maze; that the entire plot is really about freeing him, getting him to accept the idea that he and his wife did have their time together, that they did grow old together, so that Dom can achieve the catharsis he needs in order to return to his children in reality.

In "Digger", Curtis Markson is the one who is deceived - as well as many critics and viewers. And this deceit flies under the radar because unlike the rest of the film, this aspect is extremely subtle. It's easy to see why people interpret Kenny's "you're both right" speech to be Inarritu saying something like "it's true that art doesn't solve the problems it portrays, but it's still worth making", and that may in fact be the subtext. But what is it doing in the context of the film?

There are really only two monologues in the movie: the one Digger gives to the European leaders in Fossil Fools, and the one Kenny gives to Curtis Markson and the rest of the play's cast. Both speeches are given by a member of the Rockwell family, and both are meant to persuade people to go along with something despite their misgivings. This should be setting off alarm bells, and yet Curtis completely misses them. All those hours he spent watching the real Digger Rockwell, seeing how the man was not just a buffoon but a cunning sociopath, and he doesn't realize what kind of person is standing right in front of him.

Because the speech Digger gives to the European leaders is incredibly layered and Digger himself is highly charismatic. There are real issues with abandoning fossil fuels which is why the simplest thing to do is simply to keep on drilling and suffer the consequences. Likewise, there are real issues with changing the play to seriously portray how powerful and manipulative Digger really was. Is Curtis really going to blow up the performance to insist on a more realistic portrayal? Is he going to inconvenience all the people coming to see the performance and jeopardize the livelihood of everyone else involved in the play? Of course not - he can't even put it on hold until his daughter is found. He caves, just like society caved on getting off fossil fuels.

And that's why the ending of "Fossil Fools" parallels the end of the performance itself. That drawn-out sequence on the oil rig where Digger prays for food and apparently gets it, only to leap to his death once the illusion wears off, lines up with the joy and back-patting of the performance, where Curtis and everyone else is celebrating before "Level 4" returns them all to reality. Even after everything that's happened, the world is still ruled by Rockwells, because we're unable to say no to them whether that means giving up fossil fuels or insisting on artistic integrity.

**Body:** Towards the end of an interview conducted by [Dick Cavett](https://youtu.be/BdeHqesLx4s?si=VjF0ZYvZhgqU6Q7O&t=3340) Jean-Luc Goddard was asked on clarification concerning a time he sent both Diane Keaton and Robert De Niro proposals to play the same part. His thinking was that he would take whoever said *yes* first. But both Keaton and De Niro, and subsequently other people (including Cavett) who heard of this story, were puzzled & confused as to how and/or why this would work. They were unable to reconcile what Goddard wanted with what they were used to. The reverse can also be true in that Goddard made an assumption that didn't align with the reality of how filmmaking and movies worked. 

But what is interesting to me is the different viewpoints both sides had as to what character is. From this exchange a character to Goddard, as he himself explains, is like a vehicle for themes, ideas and motivations. To the other camp a character is a person; flesh and blood, only unreal in the sense that they are viewed through a screen. Thus if you were Goddard, you would have an idea or lesson you want to show, then have a framework for that character, then go on to humanise them by giving a body, age, features and so on. On the other hand, you have a human being and then you imbibe them with morals, motivations and what not. 

  
The discourse in this interview at times hovered around the differing sensibilities of American and European cinema, so its easy to think that the whole issue is simply a matter of opposite roads arriving at the same destination. But it begs the question, what do people think "playing a part" or "playing a character" really means? And do the writing/acting approaches employed in doing it matter? And why would professional performers who are experts in their craft such as De Niro and Keaton be puzzled by Goddard's request?

3. There's room for both, of course, but for myself personally either extreme feels a little silly. Though let me be clear that I don't think either side in examples here necessarily falls into these extremes; just the framing of the question kind of positions them that way.

'Character as fully-formed person' has two disadvantages. The first is that they are less malleable. As much as we might like to think of a story as characters all behaving precisely as they would from predetermined standpoint, that's very rarely so. To some degree they *are* a cog in the machine that is a story, and some stories are more character-driven and some are less so. Becoming too attached to the character as a person can be overly confining in getting a story to move from one necessary phase to another.

The second disadvantage is that a character who is too well-defined risks keeping the reader/viewer in an outsider's position looking in, rather than relating to some element of their struggle. Sometimes that's precisely what you want, but again, I'd say that's pretty rare. Even in cases where a character is not sympathetic, and not portrayed as such at all, leaving tangible gaps in who they are draws readers in and challenges them to see themselves in that situation, even when it's a situation they'd be incapable of finding themselves in. The example I've used in the past for creative writing workshops is *The Talented Mr. Ripley*. Likely the percentage of your readership that can identify with psychopath Tom Ripley is close enough to zero to be a rounding error, and if Highsmith had written him as a fleshed out monster of selfishness and malice, probably nobody would enjoy reading him. Instead, so much of who he is is left blank to the reader. We get to see him do these things, and then try desperately to finagle his way out of responsibility, and because there are gaps, we can more easily find ourselves in his head looking out, rather than keeping his crimes at arm's length as we could if we understood why he is the way he is.

At the other end of the spectrum though, character as vehicle has the same problem as the second there. Generally, you need the character to have enough of a personality framework for the audience to have something to grab onto, something that they can see in this character that they can also see in themselves. If they don't, if they're guided wholly by the needs of the plot or themes, then they feel abstracted, like pieces on a chessboard. And in ensemble stories, the chessboard can also work. "This is the Important Guy who is too hemmed in to get anything done; this is his woman whose efforts really keep him afloat; the Rook who is forthright and pushes straight to the point; the Bishop who who is a little eccentric and tip-toes around the periphery; the Knight whose reach isn't far but who covers a lot of angles; the pawns who outnumber everybody else but have no real power." But generally, you want something more for your audience to connect with than functions, because it's rare for a story abstracted to that degree to be strong enough to pull people in. 

I think the challenge then, is to find a way to flesh out your characters enough that they can feel like people when we need them to, but also leave enough of a gap for your audience to connect with them in some way. I'm a bit more of a literature than movie guy, so I often point to *Middlemarch* as an example here. *Middlemarch* is a story of many disparate character-driven threads overlapping and intersecting in a small English town. At a glance, it feels like character-as-fleshed-out-person writing, but when you take a step back, you can see how everyone seemingly maneuvers themselves to precisely where the plot needs them, and in doing so they become emblematic for kinds of struggles that people find themselves in, such that a reader can identify with probably everyone to some degree. 

I think another interesting example is *The Lord of the Rings*, in that we get the full range of characterization, from the "low," with the Hobbits exhibiting very human foibles and fears and struggles such that they feel much more fleshed out as people, up through the spectrum to Gandalf and Saruman as slightly more humanized emblematic of power directed toward good vs. power directed toward evil, and finally to the very highest end with Sauron being writ as broad, barely personified malice.
